title: 1 Samuel 9:15–27
context: The narrator reveals that the LORD had told Samuel the day before that he would send a man from Benjamin to be anointed prince over Israel, to save the people from the Philistines because their cry had reached him. When Saul appears, the LORD identifies him. Samuel invites Saul to the high place, tells him the donkeys are found, and hints that all Israel’s desire is turned toward him. Saul protests his tribe’s and family’s lowliness, but Samuel seats him in the place of honor and gives him a reserved portion. The next morning Samuel sends the servant ahead so he can tell Saul God’s message. Both traditions see here God’s gracious initiative in answering Israel’s cry, even through a king the people requested.

verses.text: Now the LORD had revealed to Samuel a day before Saul came, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the LORD had revealed his plan to Samuel a day in advance. God is not reacting in confusion to events but guiding them purposefully, while still working through the real choices of Saul, his servant, and the people along the way.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD’s advance revelation as a clear statement of his sovereign direction of events. What seemed like chance in 9:1–14 was in fact the outworking of God’s plan, which he announced to his prophet before Saul ever arrived.

verses.text: “Tomorrow about this time I will send you a man out of the land of Benjamin, and you shall anoint him to be prince over my people Israel. He will save my people out of the hand of the Philistines; for I have looked upon my people, because their cry has come to me.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers highlight that God sends the man because he has looked upon his people and their cry has come to him. God’s choice of Saul responds to real human need and prayer, showing a God who is moved by his people’s distress and acts to save them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the LORD calls Saul to save Israel because he has heard their cry, showing his covenant compassion. The people’s request in chapter 8 was sinful in motive, yet God takes it up into his own merciful purpose to deliver them from the Philistines.

verses.text: When Samuel saw Saul, the LORD said to him, “Behold, the man of whom I spoke to you! He will have authority over my people.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that God identifies Saul to Samuel and calls him the man who will have authority over his people. Saul is genuinely chosen for this office, and the rest of the story will show how he responds to the responsibility entrusted to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the LORD himself points out Saul: the choice is God’s, not merely Samuel’s or the people’s. Both traditions agree that this is a choice to an office of rule, and the narrative does not here address Saul’s personal standing before God.

verses.text: Then Saul approached Samuel in the gateway, and said, “Please tell me where the seer’s house is.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers find a touch of irony in Saul asking the seer himself where the seer’s house is. Saul does not yet know what is happening to him, and his calling comes to him unsought, inviting a response he has not yet had occasion to make.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the irony that Saul does not recognize Samuel even while speaking to him. God’s purpose is advancing before Saul is aware of it, which underlines that the initiative in this calling belongs to the LORD rather than to Saul.

verses.text: Samuel answered Saul and said, “I am the seer. Go up before me to the high place, for you are to eat with me today. In the morning I will let you go and will tell you all that is in your heart.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note Samuel’s warm welcome: Saul is to go up and eat with him, and in the morning Samuel will tell him all that is in his heart. The prophet engages Saul personally and patiently, preparing him to understand and receive the calling being offered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Samuel, as God’s messenger, knows what is in Saul’s heart and promises to disclose it. The prophet speaks with authority given by God, and the invitation to the meal begins the formal honoring of the one the LORD has chosen.

verses.text: As for your donkeys who were lost three days ago, don’t set your mind on them, for they have been found. For whom does all Israel desire? Is it not you and all your father’s house?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note Samuel’s reassurance about the donkeys, lost three days and now found, and his hint about all Israel’s desire. Saul’s small concern is set aside so that he can consider a much larger calling, which the narrative frames as an invitation he will have to embrace.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Samuel’s knowledge of the lost donkeys as confirming his prophetic insight. The question about Israel’s desire points to Saul as the answer to the people’s request in chapter 8, and they read it as God already directing events toward the king he had chosen.

verses.text: Saul answered, “Am I not a Benjamite, of the smallest of the tribes of Israel? And my family the least of all the families of the tribe of Benjamin? Why then do you speak to me like this?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Saul’s protest that Benjamin is the smallest tribe and his family the least as genuine humility at this stage. It is a promising beginning, and its later absence will mark how far Saul departs from the posture he shows here.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Saul’s protest echoes a familiar biblical pattern in which God chooses the small and unlikely, as with Gideon (Judges 6:15). Both traditions see in Saul’s words a fitting humility, though they will read his later course with different emphases.

verses.text: Samuel took Saul and his servant and brought them into the guest room, and made them sit in the best place among those who were invited, who were about thirty persons.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Samuel seats Saul and his servant in the best place among about thirty invited guests. The honor is public and generous, and it signals to Saul that his life is being turned toward a role he must now consider seriously.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Saul is given the place of honor before he has done anything to earn it. The gesture anticipates his public recognition as king and shows that the honor comes from God’s appointment communicated through his prophet.

verses.text: Samuel said to the cook, “Bring the portion which I gave you, of which I said to you, ‘Set it aside.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Samuel had planned ahead, telling the cook to set aside a special portion. The prophet acted on the LORD’s advance word, and his preparation shows how human obedience to God’s revealed plan readies the way for others to respond.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the reserved portion as another sign that Saul’s arrival was foreknown. Samuel prepared for a guest he had not yet met, because God had told him the man would come, and both traditions read the detail as underscoring the reliability of God’s word.

verses.text: The cook took up the thigh, and that which was on it, and set it before Saul. Samuel said, “Behold, that which has been reserved! Set it before yourself and eat; because it has been kept for you for the appointed time, for I said, ‘I have invited the people.’ ” So Saul ate with Samuel that day.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the honor of the thigh portion set before Saul as something kept for the appointed time. Saul eats with Samuel that day, sharing a meal that seals a relationship and marks him out, though what he becomes still depends on how he walks in the calling.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the portion was kept “for the appointed time,” stressing God’s timing. The honor reserved for Saul before he arrived shows a plan already in place, and they read the meal as a quiet sign that God had prepared this meeting in advance.

verses.text: When they had come down from the high place into the city, he talked with Saul on the housetop.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that after the meal Samuel talks with Saul on the housetop. The narrative leaves the content unstated, but the private conversation suggests patient preparation, as Samuel helps Saul begin to understand what lies ahead.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the housetop conversation, whose content is not recorded, continues Samuel’s private ministry to Saul before the anointing. The narrator’s reticence keeps the focus on the coming public word of God rather than on the details of their talk.

verses.text: They arose early; and about daybreak, Samuel called to Saul on the housetop, saying, “Get up, that I may send you away.” Saul arose, and they both went outside, he and Samuel, together.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the early rising and Samuel’s call to Saul at daybreak to send him on his way. The prophet’s urgency reflects the importance of the moment, and Saul’s readiness to rise and go out with him is a genuine response to that summons.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the daybreak summons a movement toward the decisive moment of anointing. Samuel takes the initiative, as God’s messenger, to bring Saul out of the city to hear what God has to say, keeping the focus on God’s word rather than on Saul’s plans.

verses.text: As they were going down at the end of the city, Samuel said to Saul, “Tell the servant to go on ahead of us.” He went ahead, then Samuel said, “But stand still first, that I may cause you to hear God’s message.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Samuel sends the servant ahead so that Saul can hear God’s message in private. The calling is personal, addressed to Saul himself, and it will require a personal response from him as he goes forward.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Samuel asks Saul to stand still to hear God’s message, a posture of receiving rather than acting. The anointing that follows will be God’s word and act through his prophet, and both traditions see the moment as the turning point of Saul’s life.
